title: Metals, Semiconductors, and Insulators
short_intro: Solids are classified into metals, semiconductors, and insulators based on the energy band structure formed by overlapping atomic orbitals according to Pauli's exclusion principle. The electrical behavior of these materials is governed by the occupancy of the valence band and conduction band, separated by a forbidden energy gap.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Classification of solids based on energy bands, resistivity, temperature coefficient of resistance, basic properties of conductors, intrinsic and extrinsic (p-type and n-type) semiconductors, and simple PN junction diodes.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Fermi-Dirac distribution function, Fermi energy level calculations, temperature dependence of Fermi level in intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, effective mass of charge carriers, and quantitative conductivity expressions.

prerequisites: Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom and atomic orbital overlapping
Band theory of solids (Bloch theorem concepts)

concept_notes.heading: Energy Band Formation in Solids
bullets: According to Pauli's exclusion principle, when isolated atoms are brought together to form a solid, discrete atomic energy levels split into closely spaced continuous bands.

The valence band contains the highest occupied energy levels at absolute zero temperature, while the conduction band contains unoccupied or partially occupied levels responsible for electrical conduction.
The forbidden energy gap (E<sub>g</sub>) is the energy range between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band where no electron quantum states exist.

concept_notes.heading: Metals (Conductors)
bullets: In metals, the valence band and conduction band either overlap or the conduction band is only partially filled, resulting in a zero forbidden energy gap (E<sub>g</sub> = 0).
An immense number of free electrons are available for conduction under the application of a weak electric field.
The electrical resistivity of metals increases with temperature due to increased lattice vibrations (phonon scattering), yielding a positive temperature coefficient of resistance.

concept_notes.heading: Semiconductors
bullets: Semiconductors possess a narrow forbidden energy gap, typically around E<sub>g</sub> ≈ 1.1 eV for silicon and 0.7 eV for germanium at room temperature.
At absolute zero temperature (T = 0 K), semiconductors behave as perfect insulators because the valence band is completely filled and the conduction band is empty.
As temperature increases or upon doping, covalent bonds break, generating electron-hole pairs and imparting a negative temperature coefficient of resistance.

concept_notes.heading: Insulators
bullets: Insulators feature a very large forbidden energy gap, generally E<sub>g</sub> > 3 eV (e.g., diamond has E<sub>g</sub> ≈ 5 eV).
Thermal energy at room temperature is insufficient to thermally excite electrons across such a large band gap from the valence band to the conduction band.
Insulators maintain extremely high resistivity and do not conduct electricity under normal electric field strengths.

derivations.title: Position of Fermi Level in an Intrinsic Semiconductor
steps: Write the concentration of electrons in the conduction band: n = Nc exp(-(Ec - Ef)/(kT))
Write the concentration of holes in the valence band: p = Nv exp(-(Ef - Ev)/(kT))
Equate electron and hole concentrations for an intrinsic semiconductor (n = p): Nc exp(-(Ec - Ef)/(kT)) = Nv exp(-(Ef - Ev)/(kT))
Take the natural logarithm of both sides and solve for the Fermi energy Ef: Ef = (Ec + Ev)/2 + (kT/2) ln(Nv/Nc)
derivations.result: Ef = (Ec + Ev)/2 + (kT/2) ln(Nv/Nc), which lies very close to the middle of the forbidden energy gap when effective masses of electrons and holes are nearly equal.

derivations.title: Electrical Conductivity of Semiconductors
derivations.conditions: Presence of both electrons and holes as charge carriers
steps: Express total current density J as the sum of electron and hole current densities: J = J_n + J_p = e n v_d_n + e p v_d_p
Substitute drift velocity in terms of mobility (v_d = μ E): J = e n μ_n E + e p μ_p E
Factor out the electric field E to obtain conductivity σ = J/E: σ = e (n μ_n + p μ_p)
For intrinsic semiconductors where n = p = n_i, substitute to get intrinsic conductivity: σ_i = e n_i (μ_n + μ_p)

graphs_and_experiments.title: Energy Band Diagrams of Metals, Semiconductors, and Insulators
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Three side-by-side vertical energy level schematics showing Valence Band (VB), Conduction Band (CB), and Forbidden Energy Gap (E_g). Metal: overlapping bands or partial filling (E_g = 0); Semiconductor: narrow gap (E_g ~ 1 eV); Insulator: wide gap (E_g > 3 eV).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes the availability of vacant states for electron promotion and classifies material electrical properties.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct identification questions and conceptual comparison in TGT/PGT exams.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Conductivity vs Inverse Temperature (σ vs 1/T) for Semiconductors
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A semi-log plot of ln(σ) on the y-axis against 1/T on the x-axis, showing two distinct linear slopes corresponding to intrinsic and extrinsic conduction regions.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the intrinsic region line yields the activation energy, which directly gives the band gap E_g of the semiconductor.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problems determining band gap from conductivity data at multiple temperatures.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Fermi-Dirac Distribution Function f(E) vs Energy E
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Curves of f(E) plotted against E for T = 0 K (step function dropping from 1 to 0 at E_f) and T > 0 K (smoothly curving curve passing through 0.5 at E = E_f).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the probability of occupation of an energy state by an electron at various temperatures.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual testing of Fermi energy definition and temperature effects on electron distribution.

solved_numericals.question: A piece of germanium has a forbidden energy gap of 0.72 eV. What is the maximum wavelength of electromagnetic radiation that can generate an electron-hole pair in germanium?
solution_steps: Convert band gap energy from eV to Joules: E_g = 0.72 eV = 0.72 × 1.6 × 10^-19 J = 1.152 × 10^-19 J
Use the relation between energy and wavelength: E_g = hc / λ_max

solved_numericals.question: In an intrinsic semiconductor with a band gap of 0.7 eV, calculate the probability that a state 0.35 eV above the Fermi level is occupied by an electron at temperature T = 300 K. (Take k = 8.62 × 10^-5 eV/K)
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: E - E_f = 0.35 eV, T = 300 K, k = 8.62 × 10^-5 eV/K

solved_numericals.question: An intrinsic silicon semiconductor at 300 K has carrier concentration n_i = 1.5 × 10^16 m^-3. If the electron mobility μ_n is 0.13 m^2/(V·s) and hole mobility μ_p is 0.05 m^2/(V·s), find the electrical conductivity of silicon.
solution_steps: Use the intrinsic conductivity formula: σ_i = e n_i (μ_n + μ_p)
Substitute the given values: e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, n_i = 1.5 × 10^16 m^-3, μ_n = 0.13, μ_p = 0.05

assumptions_and_limitations: Band theory assumes a periodic potential of the crystal lattice (Kronig-Penney model approximation) which neglects lattice imperfections and impurities in pure crystals.
Effective mass approximation treats electrons inside the periodic lattice as free particles with an effective mass m* that accounts for internal forces.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Semiconductors conduct better at lower temperatures because thermal agitation decreases.
common_misconceptions.correct: Semiconductors conduct better at higher temperatures.
common_misconceptions.why: Thermal energy breaks covalent bonds to generate mobile charge carriers (electron-hole pairs), overriding thermal scattering effects.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The Fermi level always lies exactly at the center of the forbidden energy gap for all semiconductors.
common_misconceptions.correct: The Fermi level lies near the center only for pure intrinsic semiconductors with nearly equal effective masses; in doped semiconductors, it shifts toward the conduction or valence band.
common_misconceptions.why: Doping alters carrier concentrations, requiring a shift in the chemical potential (Fermi level) to maintain charge neutrality.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Metals have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance.
common_misconceptions.correct: Metals have a positive temperature coefficient of resistance.
common_misconceptions.why: In metals, carrier concentration remains nearly constant while lattice vibrations increase scattering with temperature, raising resistance.

quick_revision: Metals have overlapping energy bands (E_g = 0) and positive temperature coefficients of resistance.
Semiconductors possess a narrow band gap (~1 eV) and negative temperature coefficients of resistance.
Insulators have wide band gaps (E_g > 3 eV) preventing thermal carrier excitation.
Intrinsic semiconductor conductivity depends directly on carrier concentration and mobility: σ = e n_i (μ_n + μ_p).
